definitions.statement: The imaginary unit is denoted by $i$ and satisfies $$i^{2}=-1$$ By convention, the principal square root $\sqrt{-1}$ is $i$. The equation $t^{2}=-1$ has two solutions: $t=i$ and $t=-i$.
notes: No real number has a square equal to $-1$, so $i$ is a new kind of number. It is not on the real number line.
In many classrooms in Pakistan $i$ is read as iota. Its usual name in books around the world is the imaginary unit. Both names mean the same thing.

definitions.statement: A complex number is any number that can be written as $$z=x+iy$$ where $x$ and $y$ are real numbers and $i$ is the imaginary unit. This way of writing it is called the rectangular form.
notes: Here $x$ is called the real part of $z$, and $y$ is called the imaginary part of $z$. We write $$\operatorname{Re}(z)=x, \qquad \operatorname{Im}(z)=y$$
Be careful. The imaginary part is $y$ only. The $i$ is not part of it. So for $z=5-7i$ we have $\operatorname{Im}(z)=-7$, not $-7i$.
The form $x+yi$ means the same as $x+iy$. Both are correct.
examples: For $z=-2i$: write it as $0+(-2)i$, so $\operatorname{Re}(z)=0$ and $\operatorname{Im}(z)=-2$.
For $z=6$: write it as $6+0i$, so $\operatorname{Re}(z)=6$ and $\operatorname{Im}(z)=0$.

definitions.term: Real and purely imaginary complex numbers
definitions.statement: Let $z=x+iy$, where $x$ and $y$ are real. If $y=0$, then $z$ is a real number. If $x=0$ and $y\neq 0$, then $z$ is called purely imaginary.
notes: So every real number is also a complex number. For example $7=7+0i$.
We ask for $y\neq 0$ in the second case so that $0$ is not counted as purely imaginary. The number $0$ is real.
examples: $z=9+0i$ is real, because its imaginary part is $0$.
$z=0+4i$ is purely imaginary, because its real part is $0$ and its imaginary part is not $0$.
$z=2+3i$ is neither real nor purely imaginary, because both its real and imaginary parts are nonzero.

definitions.statement: Let $z_{1}=x_{1}+iy_{1}$ and $z_{2}=x_{2}+iy_{2}$, with all four coefficients real. Then $$z_{1}=z_{2}\iff x_{1}=x_{2}\ \text{and}\ y_{1}=y_{2}$$ Thus, two complex numbers are equal if and only if their corresponding real and imaginary parts are equal.
notes: This is the rule that lets you find two unknowns. One equation between complex numbers gives you two real equations.
The rule only works when all four numbers $x_{1}$, $y_{1}$, $x_{2}$ and $y_{2}$ are real. Always check this first.
examples: If $\alpha+i\beta=-2+5i$, where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are real, then $\alpha=-2$ and $\beta=5$.
If $x+iy=7$, where $x$ and $y$ are real, then $x=7$ and $y=0$.
$3+4i\neq 4+3i$, because the real parts $3$ and $4$ are not equal.

whyItWorks.title: Why we needed a new kind of number
body: Look at $x^{2}-1=0$. Add $1$ to both sides and you get $x^{2}=1$. Two numbers work here. First $x=1$, because $1\times 1=1$. Second $x=-1$, because $(-1)\times(-1)=1$. So this equation has two real answers.
Now change one sign. Look at $x^{2}+1=0$. Take $1$ from both sides and you get $x^{2}=-1$.

Which real number works? A positive number times itself is positive, like $3\times 3=9$. A negative number times itself is also positive, like $(-3)\times(-3)=9$, because minus times minus gives plus. And $0\times 0=0$. So the square of a real number is never negative. No real number works.

You can also see this on a graph. The curve $f(x)=x^{2}-1$ cuts the $x$-axis at $(-1,0)$ and $(1,0)$, so that equation has two real answers. The curve $f(x)=x^{2}+1$ never touches the $x$-axis, so that equation has no real answer.
So mathematicians made a new number for this job. They called it $i$, and gave it one rule: $i^{2}=-1$. This defining relation lets us extend familiar algebra to complex numbers.

whyItWorks.title: Powers of $i$
body: Integer powers of $i$ follow from $i^{2}=-1$. For example, the first four positive powers are $i$, $-1$, $-i$, and $1$.
The first power of any number is the number itself, so $i^{1}=i$. The second power is the rule itself, so $i^{2}=-1$.
For the third power, take out one factor of $i$ and use the rule on what is left.$$\begin{aligned}i^{3} &= i^{2}\cdot i \\ &= (-1)\cdot i \\ &= -i\end{aligned}$$
For the fourth power, write it as the square of $i^{2}$.$$\begin{aligned}i^{4} &= \left(i^{2}\right)^{2} \\ &= (-1)^{2} \\ &= 1\end{aligned}$$

For a nonnegative integer exponent, an even power has the form $2k$, while an odd power has the form $2k+1$, with $k$ a nonnegative integer. Write $i^{2k}=(i^{2})^{k}$; in an odd power, leave one factor of $i$ outside.
You are then left with $(-1)^{k}$, which is easy to read off. It is $1$ when $k$ is even and $-1$ when $k$ is odd, because minus signs cancel in pairs and an odd one is always left over.

rule.example: Take $i^{23}$. It is odd, and $23=2(11)+1$, so $i^{23}=\left(i^{2}\right)^{11}\cdot i=(-1)^{11}\cdot i=-i$, because $11$ is odd.

whyItWorks.title: Negative powers and the reciprocal of $i$
body: For a nonzero number $a$ and a positive integer $n$, a negative exponent means a reciprocal: $$a^{-n}=\frac{1}{a^{n}}$$ In particular, $i^{-n}=1/i^{n}$ because $i\neq0$.
After simplifying the denominator, we may obtain $1/i$ or $1/(-i)$. These are valid exact expressions. To write them in rectangular form, replace the imaginary denominator with a real one.

To clear it, multiply the top and the bottom by $i$. You may do this because $\frac{i}{i}=1$, and multiplying by $1$ changes how a number looks but not its value.$$\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{i} &= \frac{1}{i}\times\frac{i}{i} \\ &= \frac{1\times i}{i\times i} \\ &= \frac{i}{i^{2}} \\ &= \frac{i}{-1} \\ &= -i\end{aligned}$$
Read the last line slowly. Dividing by $-1$ is the same as multiplying by $-1$. It just changes the sign.

whyItWorks.title: Square roots of negative numbers
body: Let $a$ be a positive number. To write $\sqrt{-a}$ using $i$, first pull the minus sign out as a factor of $-1$.$$\begin{aligned}\sqrt{-a} &= \sqrt{a\times(-1)} \\ &= \sqrt{a}\times\sqrt{-1} \\ &= i\sqrt{a}\end{aligned}$$

Here $a>0$, and we use the specific principal-root identity $\sqrt{-a}=\sqrt{a}\,\sqrt{-1}=i\sqrt{a}$. Do not extend the real product rule to two negative factors: $\sqrt{-1}\sqrt{-1}=-1$, whereas $\sqrt{(-1)(-1)}=1$.
For example $\sqrt{-4}=\sqrt{4}\times\sqrt{-1}=2i$, because $\sqrt{4}=2$. And $\sqrt{-7}=i\sqrt{7}$. Here $\sqrt{7}$ must stay as it is, because $7$ is not a perfect square.
Both $i\sqrt{7}$ and $\sqrt{7}\,i$ are correct. We prefer $i\sqrt{7}$ in our working to make it clear that $i$ is outside the radical. Neither expression means $\sqrt{7i}$.

history.title: From the number line to the complex plane
body: A real number can be represented on a line. A complex number needs two real coordinates: $x$ gives its horizontal position, and $y$ gives its vertical position.

The geometric interpretation was developed independently by several mathematicians. Wessel published a plane interpretation in 1799; Argand developed his independent account in 1806. Their work helps explain why complex numbers are represented as points, not as positions on the real number line.

definitions.statement: If $z=x+iy$ and $k$ is real, then $$kz=k(x+iy)=kx+i(ky)$$ Multiply both coordinates by the same real number.
notes: For $z\neq0$ and $k>0$, the direction of the arrow from the origin stays the same and its length is multiplied by $k$. For $k<0$, the arrow points in the opposite direction and its length is multiplied by $|k|$. If $k=0$ or $z=0$, the result is the origin.

definitions.statement: Let $z_{1}=x_{1}+iy_{1}$ and $z_{2}=x_{2}+iy_{2}$, with real coordinates. Addition and subtraction act on corresponding parts: $$\begin{aligned}z_{1}+z_{2}&=(x_{1}+x_{2})+i(y_{1}+y_{2}), \\ z_{1}-z_{2}&=(x_{1}-x_{2})+i(y_{1}-y_{2})\end{aligned}$$
notes: In words: add the real parts together, and add the imaginary parts together. Real parts and imaginary parts never mix.
This is the same as collecting like terms in algebra. The numbers without $i$ are one kind of term, and the numbers with $i$ are another.
The formula can be derived: expand the brackets term by term, replace $i^{2}$ by $-1$, and collect corresponding terms.
The minus sign in $x_{1}x_{2}-y_{1}y_{2}$ comes from $i^{2}=-1$. It is not an extra rule to learn.

definitions.statement: Let $z_{1}=x_{1}+iy_{1}$ and $z_{2}=x_{2}+iy_{2}$, with real coordinates and $z_{2}\neq0$. Multiply the numerator and denominator by $\bar z_{2}=x_{2}-iy_{2}$: $$\frac{z_{1}}{z_{2}}=\frac{(x_{1}+iy_{1})(x_{2}-iy_{2})}{x_{2}^{2}+y_{2}^{2}}$$ Expanding the numerator gives $$\frac{z_{1}}{z_{2}}=\frac{x_{1}x_{2}+y_{1}y_{2}}{x_{2}^{2}+y_{2}^{2}}+i\frac{y_{1}x_{2}-x_{1}y_{2}}{x_{2}^{2}+y_{2}^{2}}$$
notes: The method is what matters: multiply the top and the bottom by the conjugate of the bottom. The conjugate of $x+iy$ is $x-iy$.
This works because $(x+iy)(x-iy)=x^{2}+y^{2}$, which is an ordinary real number. The $i$ disappears from the denominator.
Since $z_{2}\neq0$, its conjugate is also nonzero and $x_{2}^{2}+y_{2}^{2}>0$. Thus the fraction used to multiply numerator and denominator equals $1$.

definitions.statement: The additive inverse of $z$ is the number $-z$ that you add to $z$ to get $0$: $$z+(-z)=0$$ For $z=x+iy$, the additive inverse is $-z=-x-iy$.
notes: Change the sign of both parts, not just one. This is a common mistake in the whole exercise.
The number $0=0+0i$ is called the additive identity, because $z+0=z$ for every complex number $z$.

definitions.statement: For $z\neq 0$, the multiplicative inverse of $z$ is the number $z^{-1}$ that you multiply $z$ by to get $1$: $$z\,z^{-1}=1, \qquad z^{-1}=\frac{1}{z}$$
notes: To find it, write $\frac{1}{z}$ and then clear the $i$ from the denominator with the conjugate, exactly as in division.
For $z=x+iy$ this gives $z^{-1}=\frac{x}{x^{2}+y^{2}}-i\,\frac{y}{x^{2}+y^{2}}$.
The number $1=1+0i$ is called the multiplicative identity, because $z\times 1=z$ for every complex number $z$.
Only $0$ has no multiplicative inverse, because you cannot divide by $0$.
examples: The multiplicative inverse of $i$ is $-i$, because $i\times(-i)=-i^{2}=1$.

definitions.statement: For all complex numbers $z_{1}$, $z_{2}$ and $z_{3}$, addition and multiplication both satisfy closure, the commutative property and the associative property, each has an identity, and multiplication is distributive over addition.
notes: Closure: $z_{1}+z_{2}$ and $z_{1}z_{2}$ are again complex numbers.
Commutative: $z_{1}+z_{2}=z_{2}+z_{1}$ and $z_{1}z_{2}=z_{2}z_{1}$. Order does not matter.
Associative: $(z_{1}+z_{2})+z_{3}=z_{1}+(z_{2}+z_{3})$ and $(z_{1}z_{2})z_{3}=z_{1}(z_{2}z_{3})$. Grouping does not matter.
Identities: $z+0=z$ and $z\times 1=z$.

whyItWorks.title: Addition and subtraction on the complex plane
body: The number $x+iy$ corresponds to the point $(x,y)$ and to the arrow from the origin to that point. To add two numbers geometrically, place the tail of the second arrow at the head of the first, without changing its direction or length.

The final endpoint has coordinates $(x_{1}+x_{2},y_{1}+y_{2})$. This is the same coordinate addition used in the algebraic rule. If the arrows are parallel, the usual parallelogram picture becomes a line segment, but the coordinate rule still works.
To subtract $z_{2}$, add $-z_{2}$ instead. Negating a number reverses both coordinates, so the arrow is turned through $180^\circ$ about the origin. For example, $-(2-3i)=-2+3i$.

whyItWorks.title: Why multiplying is just ordinary algebra
body: Multiply two brackets the way you always have. Each term in the first multiplies each term in the second, giving four products.
Only the last term is new. It carries $i^{2}$, and $i^{2}=-1$, so that term becomes $-y_{1}y_{2}$, a real number with no $i$ on it.

Now collect. The terms without $i$ are $x_{1}x_{2}$ and $-y_{1}y_{2}$. The terms with $i$ are $ix_{1}y_{2}$ and $iy_{1}x_{2}$.$$\begin{aligned}z_{1}z_{2} &= (x_{1}x_{2}-y_{1}y_{2})+i(x_{1}y_{2}+y_{1}x_{2})\end{aligned}$$
That is the whole formula. You can reconstruct the formula by expanding the brackets and using $i^{2}=-1$.

whyItWorks.title: Why the conjugate clears the denominator
body: The fraction $\frac{3+4i}{5-7i}$ is already a valid complex number. The task is to rewrite it in rectangular form, with a real denominator, so its real and imaginary parts are explicit.
The trick is to multiply the top and the bottom by the conjugate of the bottom. The conjugate of $5-7i$ is $5+7i$: same real part, opposite sign on the imaginary part.

Look at what the bottom becomes. It is of the form $(a-b)(a+b)$, which is always $a^{2}-b^{2}$.$$\begin{aligned}(5-7i)(5+7i) &= 5^{2}-(7i)^{2} \\ &= 25-49i^{2} \\ &= 25-49(-1) \\ &= 25+49 = 74\end{aligned}$$
Read the third line carefully. Because $i^{2}=-1$, the subtraction turns into an addition, and the answer is a plain positive number with no $i$ in it at all. That is exactly what we wanted.
In general $(x+iy)(x-iy)=x^{2}+y^{2}$, which is always real and never negative.
You are allowed to multiply top and bottom because $\frac{5+7i}{5+7i}=1$, and multiplying by $1$ changes how a number looks but not its value.

whyItWorks.title: The two inverses are different things
body: Students mix these up, so hold them apart.
The additive inverse undoes addition. You add it to $z$ and land on $0$, the additive identity. For $z=x+iy$ it is $-x-iy$. Both signs change, and no division is needed.

The multiplicative inverse undoes multiplication. You multiply $z$ by it and land on $1$, the multiplicative identity. It is $\frac{1}{z}$ for $z\neq0$. The conjugate method rewrites this reciprocal in rectangular form.

A quick check for the multiplicative inverse: multiply your answer by $z$ and see whether you get $1$.$$\begin{aligned}(4-3i)\left(\frac{4}{25}+\frac{3}{25}i\right) &= \frac{(4-3i)(4+3i)}{25} \\ &= \frac{16+9}{25} \\ &= 1 \quad \checkmark\end{aligned}$$
Every complex number has an additive inverse. Every complex number except $0$ has a multiplicative inverse, because you cannot divide by $0$.

history.title: Which algebraic rules still apply?
body: Complex addition and multiplication preserve the commutative, associative, and distributive laws. That is why expanding brackets, collecting terms, and solving linear equations still work.

Not every rule for real numbers transfers unchanged. Complex numbers do not have a compatible order like the real number line, and the square-root product rule needs care. Always keep the hypotheses of the rule being used.

definitions.statement: A complex number $z=x+iy$ is fixed by the ordered pair of real numbers $(x,y)$, so it can be drawn as the point $(x,y)$ in a plane. The horizontal axis carries the real part and is called the real axis. The vertical axis carries the imaginary part and is called the imaginary axis. This plane is called the complex plane, or the Argand plane.
notes: A complex number can also be drawn as an arrow from the origin to that point. The number, the point and the arrow are all written with the same letter $z$.
The plane is named after Jean Robert Argand $(1768$ to $1822)$, a Swiss mathematician.
examples: $8$ is the point $(8,0)$, which lies on the real axis, because its imaginary part is $0$.
$-7i$ is the point $(0,-7)$, which lies on the imaginary axis, because its real part is $0$.

definitions.statement: The conjugate of $z=x+iy$ is written $\bar{z}$ and is defined by $$\bar{z}=x-iy$$ In words: keep the real part exactly as it is, and change the sign of the imaginary part.
notes: In rectangular form with real coefficients, replace $x+iy$ by $x-iy$. The real part stays unchanged.
Conjugation reflects a point across the real axis. A point above the axis moves the same distance below it, and conversely. A point on the real axis stays where it is.
The product of a complex number with its conjugate is always a real number. This is what makes the conjugate useful for division.
examples: The conjugate of $6$ is $6$, because its imaginary part is already $0$.

definitions.statement: For complex numbers $z$, $z_{1}$, and $z_{2}$, $$\begin{aligned}\overline{z_{1}+z_{2}}&=\bar z_{1}+\bar z_{2}, \\ \overline{z_{1}z_{2}}&=\bar z_{1}\bar z_{2}, \\ \overline{\left(\frac{z_{1}}{z_{2}}\right)}&=\frac{\bar z_{1}}{\bar z_{2}}\quad(z_{2}\neq0), \\ \overline{\bar z}&=z\end{aligned}$$
notes: In words: taking the conjugate can be done before or after adding, multiplying or dividing, and the answer is the same either way.
The last one says that taking the conjugate twice brings you back to where you started. Reflecting in the real axis twice returns the point to its original place.

definitions.statement: The modulus of $z=x+iy$ is written $|z|$ and is defined by $$|z|=\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}$$
notes: The modulus is the distance from the origin to the point $(x,y)$. The horizontal and vertical distances are $|x|$ and $|y|$, not possibly negative coordinates. Pythagoras gives $|z|^{2}=x^{2}+y^{2}$; the formula also holds on either axis and at the origin.
A modulus is a nonnegative real number, and $|z|=0$ if and only if $z=0$.
Square each part before adding. Note that $|3-4i|$ is $\sqrt{9+16}=5$, not $3-4$.
For a real number this is just the size without the sign, which is why the same two bars are used.

definitions.statement: For any complex number $z=x+iy$, $$|z|=|\bar{z}|=|{-z}|=|{-\bar{z}}|=\left|\bar{\bar{z}}\right|, \qquad z\bar{z}=|z|^{2}$$
notes: The first chain says that changing signs does not change distance. Every one of $z$, $\bar{z}$, $-z$ and $-\bar{z}$ has the same two numbers being squared, so the sum $x^{2}+y^{2}$ is the same for all of them.
The identity $z\bar z=|z|^{2}$ explains why multiplication by the conjugate produces a real denominator. This denominator is strictly positive when $z\neq0$.
Note carefully that $z\bar{z}$ gives $|z|^{2}$, not $|z|$. There is no square root at the end.

whyItWorks.title: Why conjugation preserves sums
body: Let $z_{1}=a+bi$ and $z_{2}=c+di$, where $a,b,c,d$ are real. Add first and then conjugate:
$$\begin{aligned}\overline{z_{1}+z_{2}}&=\overline{(a+c)+(b+d)i} \\ &=(a+c)-(b+d)i\end{aligned}$$
Conjugating first and then adding gives the same expression:
$$\begin{aligned}\bar z_{1}+\bar z_{2}&=(a-bi)+(c-di) \\ &=(a+c)-(b+d)i\end{aligned}$$
Thus $\overline{z_{1}+z_{2}}=\bar z_{1}+\bar z_{2}$ for every pair of complex numbers, not just for one numerical example.

whyItWorks.title: Why conjugation preserves products
body: For the same real coordinates, multiplication gives $z_{1}z_{2}=(ac-bd)+(ad+bc)i$. Consequently,
$$\begin{aligned}\overline{z_{1}z_{2}}&=(ac-bd)-(ad+bc)i\end{aligned}$$
Now multiply the conjugates directly:
$$\begin{aligned}\bar z_{1}\bar z_{2}&=(a-bi)(c-di) \\ &=ac-adi-bci+bd\,i^{2} \\ &=(ac-bd)-(ad+bc)i\end{aligned}$$
The two results agree, so $\overline{z_{1}z_{2}}=\bar z_{1}\bar z_{2}$.

whyItWorks.title: Why conjugation preserves quotients
body: Assume $z_{2}\neq0$ and let $w=z_{1}/z_{2}$. Then $wz_{2}=z_{1}$. Conjugate both sides and use the product property just proved:
$$\begin{aligned}\overline{wz_{2}}&=\bar z_{1}, \\ \bar w\,\bar z_{2}&=\bar z_{1}\end{aligned}$$
The conjugate $\bar z_{2}$ is nonzero: if it were $0$, both real coordinates of $z_{2}$ would be $0$. Divide by $\bar z_{2}$ to obtain
$$\begin{aligned}\overline{\left(\frac{z_{1}}{z_{2}}\right)}&=\frac{\bar z_{1}}{\bar z_{2}}\end{aligned}$$

whyItWorks.title: Why conjugating twice returns the number
body: If $z=x+iy$ with $x,y$ real, its conjugate is $x-iy=x+i(-y)$. A second conjugation changes $-y$ back to $y$:
$$\begin{aligned}\overline{\bar z}&=x-i(-y) \\ &=x+iy \\ &=z\end{aligned}$$

whyItWorks.title: Why the modulus is a distance
body: Draw $z=x+iy$ as the point $P(x,y)$. Draw a perpendicular from $P$ to the real axis, meeting it at $M=(x,0)$. Depending on the sign of $y$, this segment goes upward or downward.

When $x$ and $y$ are both nonzero, $OMP$ is a right triangle. Its horizontal and vertical side lengths are $|x|$ and $|y|$, not possibly negative coordinates. Since $|x|^{2}=x^{2}$ and $|y|^{2}=y^{2}$, Pythagoras gives the formula below. If either coordinate is $0$, the same formula gives the distance along an axis.
For the nondegenerate triangle, Pythagoras gives $$\begin{aligned}OP^{2}&=OM^{2}+MP^{2} \\ &=|x|^{2}+|y|^{2} \\ &=x^{2}+y^{2}\end{aligned}$$
Take the square root of both sides, and take the nonnegative root, because a distance is never negative.$$\begin{aligned}OP &= \sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}} = |z|\end{aligned}$$
At the origin, both coordinates and the distance are $0$. Thus the same formula covers every point in the complex plane.

whyItWorks.title: Why $|z|$, $|\bar{z}|$, $|{-z}|$ and $|{-\bar{z}}|$ are all equal
body: Write the four numbers out side by side and see what changes.$$\begin{aligned}z &= x+iy \\ \bar{z} &= x-iy \\ -z &= -x-iy \\ -\bar{z} &= -x+iy\end{aligned}$$
Only the signs change. The real part is $x$ or $-x$, and the imaginary part is $y$ or $-y$.
Now put each one into the modulus formula. Squaring destroys a minus sign, because minus times minus gives plus.$$\begin{aligned}(-x)^{2} &= x^{2} \\ (-y)^{2} &= y^{2}\end{aligned}$$
So every one of the four gives the same sum inside the root, namely $x^{2}+y^{2}$, and therefore the same modulus.
The complex plane gives a geometric explanation. Reflecting a point in an axis, or turning it through $180^\circ$ about the origin, never changes how far it is from the origin.

whyItWorks.title: Why $z\bar{z}=|z|^{2}$
body: Take $z=x+iy$, so that $\bar{z}=x-iy$, and multiply them. The two brackets are of the form $(a+b)(a-b)$, which is always $a^{2}-b^{2}$, with $a=x$ and $b=iy$.$$\begin{aligned}z\bar{z} &= (x+iy)(x-iy) \\ &= x^{2}-(iy)^{2}\end{aligned}$$
Now open the second square. Square both the $i$ and the $y$.$$\begin{aligned}(iy)^{2} &= i^{2}y^{2} \\ &= (-1)y^{2} = -y^{2}\end{aligned}$$
Subtract it. Taking away $-y^{2}$ is the same as adding $y^{2}$.$$\begin{aligned}z\bar{z} &= x^{2}-(-y^{2}) \\ &= x^{2}+y^{2}\end{aligned}$$
But $x^{2}+y^{2}$ is exactly what sits inside the square root in the modulus, so it is $|z|^{2}$.$$\begin{aligned}|z|^{2} &= \left(\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}\right)^{2} = x^{2}+y^{2}\end{aligned}$$
So $z\bar{z}=|z|^{2}$. Two things follow. The product is always real, which is why the conjugate clears a denominator. And it is never negative, which fits a squared distance.

history.title: The Argand diagram
body: Caspar Wessel published a geometric interpretation of complex numbers in 1799. Jean-Robert Argand developed an independent account in 1806; the name Argand diagram is commonly used for the complex plane.
The same diagram connects the algebraic ideas in this unit: conjugation is reflection across the real axis, negation is a half-turn about the origin, and modulus is distance from the origin.

definitions.term: Real and imaginary parts of a power
definitions.statement: Let $z=(x+iy)^{n}$, with $x,y$ real and $n\in\{1,-1,2,-2\}$. If $n<0$, assume $x+iy\neq0$. Rewrite $z$ as $u+iv$, with $u,v$ real. Then $$\operatorname{Re}(z)=u,\qquad\operatorname{Im}(z)=v$$ The real and imaginary parts exist before the rewriting; the calculation makes their values explicit.
notes: The $i$ is never part of the imaginary part. For $z=55-48i$, $\operatorname{Im}(z)=-48$, not $-48i$.
For a nonzero base and a positive integer $n$, $(x+iy)^{-n}=1/(x+iy)^{n}$. A negative exponent means a reciprocal, not a minus sign in front of the answer.
For $n=-1$ the imaginary part carries a minus sign, because the conjugate on top is $x-iy$.

definitions.statement: To identify the parts of a power of a quotient, rewrite the result in rectangular form. You may simplify the quotient first. For a negative power, taking the reciprocal first is often shorter; then simplify that quotient and apply the remaining positive power. The original denominator must be nonzero, and for a negative power the original numerator must also be nonzero.
notes: If $p\neq0$ and $q\neq0$, then $\left(\frac pq\right)^{-1}=\frac qp$. Both restrictions matter: the original quotient and its reciprocal must be defined.
A power of $-2$ turns the fraction upside down and then squares it.
Once the number is in the form $x+iy$, the real part is $x$ and the imaginary part is $y$.

definitions.term: Real and imaginary parts from the conjugate
definitions.statement: The two parts can also be read from the number and its conjugate: $$\operatorname{Re}(z)=\frac{z+\bar{z}}{2}, \qquad \operatorname{Im}(z)=\frac{z-\bar{z}}{2i}$$
notes: Adding $z$ and $\bar{z}$ cancels the imaginary parts and doubles the real part. Subtracting them cancels the real parts and leaves twice the imaginary term.
This is mostly useful as a check. Simplifying the number to the form $x+iy$ is usually the quicker route.

definitions.term: Simultaneous linear equations with complex coefficients
definitions.statement: A system of simultaneous equations asks for values of the unknowns that satisfy every equation in the system. Linear systems with complex coefficients can be solved by substitution or elimination, using the same algebraic laws as for real coefficients.
notes: In substitution, express one unknown in terms of the other, substitute, solve the resulting equation, and substitute back. In elimination, add or subtract suitable multiples of the equations to remove one unknown.
The working is the same as for real equations. The one extra move is clearing $i$ from a denominator with the conjugate whenever a division appears.
Choose the equation and the unknown that are simplest to isolate, usually one with coefficient $1$ or $-1$.
Put both answers back into both original equations to check.
examples: The system $5z-(3+i)w=7-i$ and $(2-i)z+2iw=4$ has the solution $z=2$ and $w=1$.
The system $z-4w=3i$ and $2z+3w=11-5i$ has the solution $z=4-i$ and $w=1-i$.

whyItWorks.title: Reading the parts after simplification
body: The real part and the imaginary part are names for the two pieces of a number written as $x+iy$: one plain real number, then a real number times $i$.
The expressions $(8-3i)^{2}$ and $(4+3i)^{-1}$ have real and imaginary parts, but these are not simply the coordinates written inside the original brackets.

Multiplying the bracket out, or clearing the $i$ from a denominator, does not change the number. It only rewrites it in the standard shape.$$\begin{aligned}(8-3i)^{2} &= 8^{2}-2(8)(3i)+(3i)^{2} \\ &= 64-48i+9i^{2} \\ &= 64-48i-9 \\ &= 55-48i\end{aligned}$$
Now that it reads $55-48i$, the real part is $55$ and the imaginary part is $-48$. These parts existed throughout; rewriting makes them easy to read.

whyItWorks.title: Why $(x+iy)^{-1}$ has the parts it does
body: Assume $x,y$ are real and $x+iy\neq0$. Start from the meaning of a negative exponent: $$\begin{aligned}z&=(x+iy)^{-1}=\frac{1}{x+iy}\end{aligned}$$

There is an $i$ in the denominator, so this is not the form $x+iy$. Multiply the top and the bottom by the conjugate $x-iy$. You may do this because $\frac{x-iy}{x-iy}=1$, and multiplying by $1$ changes how a number looks but not its value.$$\begin{aligned}z &= \frac{1}{x+iy}\times\frac{x-iy}{x-iy}\end{aligned}$$
The denominator is of the form $(x+iy)(x-iy)$, which is $x^{2}-(iy)^{2}=x^{2}+y^{2}$, an ordinary real number with no $i$ in it.$$\begin{aligned}z &= \frac{x-iy}{x^{2}+y^{2}}\end{aligned}$$
Split the one fraction into two, one for each part.$$\begin{aligned}z &= \frac{x}{x^{2}+y^{2}} - \frac{y}{x^{2}+y^{2}}\,i\end{aligned}$$
So $\operatorname{Re}(z)=\frac{x}{x^{2}+y^{2}}$ and $\operatorname{Im}(z)=\frac{-y}{x^{2}+y^{2}}$. The minus sign sits on the imaginary part, because the conjugate on top was $x-iy$.

whyItWorks.title: The parts of a square and a reciprocal square
body: Let $a=x+iy$, where $x,y$ are real. Expanding the square gives
Thus $\operatorname{Re}(a^{2})=x^{2}-y^{2}$ and $\operatorname{Im}(a^{2})=2xy$.
For $a\neq0$, use $a^{-1}=(x-iy)/(x^{2}+y^{2})$ and square both the numerator and the denominator:
The denominator is positive because $x^{2}+y^{2}>0$. Therefore,
$$\begin{aligned}\operatorname{Re}(a^{-2})&=\frac{x^{2}-y^{2}}{(x^{2}+y^{2})^{2}}, \\ \operatorname{Im}(a^{-2})&=-\frac{2xy}{(x^{2}+y^{2})^{2}}\end{aligned}$$

whyItWorks.title: Why substitution solves a system with complex coefficients
body: Two equations may determine two unknowns, but the equations must provide independent, consistent information. They can also have no solution or infinitely many solutions.
Making $w$ the subject of one equation turns the other equation into a single equation whose only unknown is $z$.

In the examples here, elimination leaves a nonzero coefficient of the remaining unknown, so division gives one value. If the coefficient were $0$, we would first check whether the resulting equation is an identity or a contradiction.
With $z$ known, the rearranged first equation hands you $w$ straight away.
For example, from $5z-(3+i)w=7-i$ we get $w=\frac{5z-7+i}{3+i}$. Putting this into $(2-i)z+2iw=4$ and clearing the fraction leads to $z(7+9i)=2(7+9i)$, so $z=2$, and then $w=\frac{3+i}{3+i}=1$.

whyItWorks.title: Recovering the two parts from conjugates
body: If $z=x+iy$, then $\bar z=x-iy$. Addition cancels the imaginary terms, while subtraction cancels the real terms:
$$\begin{aligned}z+\bar z&=(x+iy)+(x-iy)=2x, \\ z-\bar z&=(x+iy)-(x-iy)=2iy\end{aligned}$$
Divide the first equation by $2$ and the second by $2i$. Both divisors are nonzero, so
$$\begin{aligned}\operatorname{Re}(z)&=\frac{z+\bar z}{2}, \\ \operatorname{Im}(z)&=\frac{z-\bar z}{2i}\end{aligned}$$

Add $(3+i)w$ to both sides and take $7-i$ from both sides, so the $w$ term is by itself.
Divide both sides by $3+i$ to make $w$ the subject. Call this equation $(3)$.
Put this expression for $w$ into equation $(2)$.
Multiply every term by $3+i$ to clear the fraction.
Work out $(2-i)(3+i)$ term by term.
Replace $i^{2}$ by $-1$ and collect. $-i^{2}=1$, so $6+1=7$, and $2i-3i=-i$.
Work out $2i(5z-7+i)$. The last term is $2i^{2}=-2$.
Put these back. The right side is $4(3+i)=12+4i$.
Add $14i+2$ to both sides, so the two $z$ terms stand alone on the left.
Add the two $z$ terms. $(7-i)+10i=7+9i$.
The right side is $2(7+9i)$, so divide both sides by $7+9i$.
Put $z=2$ into equation $(3)$.
Work out the top. $10-7+i=3+i$, which is the same as the bottom.
State both answers.

First expand $(2-i)(3+i)$.

Put both back, with $4(3+i)=12+4i$ on the right.
Put $z=2$ back into equation $(3)$.

questions.stem: Answer the following in your own words.

parts.label: (i)
parts.question: Is $0$ a complex number? Explain.
parts.answer: Yes. $0=0+0i$, so it is a complex number, and it is also a real number.

steps.why: A complex number is any number that can be written as $x+iy$, where $x$ and $y$ are real numbers. So the test is simply whether $0$ can be written in that shape.
It can. Take $x=0$ and $y=0$.
So $0$ is a complex number. Because its imaginary part is $0$, it is a real number as well. Every real number is a complex number whose imaginary part happens to be $0$.

written.say: A complex number has the form $x+iy$ with $x,y\in\mathbb R$. Choose $x=0$ and $y=0$.
So $0$ is complex. Its imaginary coefficient is $0$, so it is also real.

notes.watchOut: $0$ is not purely imaginary. A purely imaginary number needs $x=0$ and $y\neq 0$, and here $y=0$.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.question: What is the result of multiplying a complex number by its conjugate?
parts.answer: A real number, equal to $x^{2}+y^{2}$, which is $|z|^{2}$.

steps.why: Let the number be $z=x+iy$, where $x$ and $y$ are real. Its conjugate keeps the real part and changes the sign of the imaginary part.
Multiply them. The two brackets are of the form $(a+b)(a-b)$, which always gives $a^{2}-b^{2}$. Here $a=x$ and $b=iy$.
Square the second term. Square both the $i$ and the $y$, then use $i^{2}=-1$.
Subtract. Taking away $-y^{2}$ is the same as adding $y^{2}$.
Both $x^{2}$ and $y^{2}$ are real, so the answer is always real. It is also never negative, and it equals the square of the modulus.

written.say: Let $z=x+iy$, where $x,y\in\mathbb R$. Then $\bar z=x-iy$.

written.math: \begin{aligned}z\bar z &= (x+iy)(x-iy) \\ &= x^2-(iy)^2 && \textcolor{#40516D}{\small (a+b)(a-b)=a^2-b^2} \\ &= x^2-i^2y^2 \\ &= x^2-(-1)y^2 && \textcolor{#40516D}{\small i^2=-1} \\ &= x^2+y^2\end{aligned}

written.say: The sum of these real squares is nonnegative and is the square of the modulus.

parts.answer: Their real parts must be equal and their imaginary parts must be equal.

In the denominator, $-i=(-1)\cdot i$. Separate the two factors.
Take out one factor of $i$, then use $i^2=-1$.

written.math: \begin{aligned}i^{9} &= i^{8}\cdot i \\ &= (i^2)^{4}\cdot i && \textcolor{#40516D}{\small a^{mn}=(a^m)^n} \\ &= (-1)^{4}\cdot i && \textcolor{#40516D}{\small i^2=-1} \\ &= 1\cdot i && \textcolor{#40516D}{\small (-1)^k=1\text{ for even }k} \\ &= i\end{aligned}

written.say: Since $9$ is odd, $(-1)^{9}=-1$. Substitute both reduced factors.
Now substitute into the reciprocal and simplify.

steps.why: Multiply the brackets term by term. Each term in the first bracket multiplies each term in the second, giving four products.
Work out each product. In the last one, minus times minus gives plus, and $4\cdot 6=24$.
Replace $i^{2}$ by $-1$ in the last term.
Now collect the real numbers together and the $i$ terms together.
Taking $24$ from $15$ goes $9$ below $0$. And $-18-20=-38$.

written.say: Multiply each term in the first bracket by each term in the second.

steps.why: Division is written as a fraction.
There is $i$ at the bottom, so this is not a finished answer. Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the bottom, which is $5+7i$. This is allowed because that fraction equals $1$.
Take the bottom first. It is of the form $(a-b)(a+b)=a^{2}-b^{2}$, and $i^{2}=-1$ turns the subtraction into an addition.
Now the top, multiplying term by term.
Replace $i^{2}$ by $-1$ and collect. The real numbers give $15-28=-13$, and the $i$ terms give $21+20=41$.
Put the top over the bottom.

written.say: Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate $5+7i$.
Expand the numerator first.
Multiply the conjugate pair using the difference of squares.
Substitute the numerator and denominator, then simplify to rectangular form.

notes.alsoAcceptable: $-\frac{13}{74}+\frac{41}{74}i$ is equally correct and shows the two parts separately.

questions.stem: Find the additive and multiplicative inverse of $z=8+9i$.

steps.why: Two different inverses are wanted, so take them one at a time. The additive inverse is the number you add to $z$ to get $0$, and it is written $-z$.
To find it, put a minus in front of the whole number. A minus in front of a bracket changes the sign of every term inside.
Change the sign of both parts. The real part $8$ becomes $-8$, and the imaginary part $+9$ becomes $-9$.
Now the multiplicative inverse. It is the number you multiply $z$ by to get $1$, written $z^{-1}$, and it equals $\frac{1}{z}$.
The reciprocal is correct; next write it in rectangular form. Multiply the top and the bottom by the conjugate of the bottom, which is $8-9i$.
Work out the denominator. The two brackets are of the form $(a+b)(a-b)$, which is always $a^{2}-b^{2}$.
Square each part. Since $(9i)^{2}=81i^{2}=-81$, taking it away adds $81$.
The numerator is just $8-9i$, because the top was $1$.
Split it into a real part and an imaginary part.
State both inverses together.

written.say: The additive inverse changes both signs, so that its sum with the original number is $0$.
For the multiplicative inverse, use the reciprocal instead. Write the reciprocal and use the conjugate $8-9i$.
Multiply the conjugate pair using the difference of squares.
Substitute the numerator and denominator, then simplify to rectangular form.

notes.watchOut: These are two different things. The additive inverse needs no division at all, and only the multiplicative inverse needs the conjugate.

questions.stem: If $z_{1}=3+4i$ and $z_{2}=2+3i$, then verify that:

parts.label: (i)
parts.question: $\overline{z_{1}+z_{2}}=\bar{z_{1}}+\bar{z_{2}}$
parts.answer: Both sides give $5-7i$, so the property holds.

steps.why: To verify, work out each side on its own and show they agree. Never assume they are equal. The left side says add first, then take the conjugate, so add the parts separately.
Now take the conjugate of that sum, keeping the real part and changing the sign of the imaginary part.
The right side says take the conjugates first. Write each one.
Add them, part by part. The imaginary parts give $-4-3=-7$, because going down $3$ more from $-4$ reaches $-7$.
From $(1)$ and $(2)$ both sides give the same number.

written.say: Calculate the left side first: perform the operation before conjugating. Add the real coefficients and the imaginary coefficients separately.
Take the conjugate of this result.
For the right side, conjugate the two inputs first.
Add the real coefficients and the imaginary coefficients separately.
Both sides give $5-7i$, so the required equality holds for these values.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.question: $\overline{z_{1}z_{2}}=\bar{z_{1}}\,\bar{z_{2}}$
parts.answer: Both sides give $-6-17i$, so the property holds.

steps.why: The left side says multiply first, then take the conjugate. Multiply the brackets out term by term.
Collect. The real numbers give $6-12=-6$, and the $i$ terms give $9i+8i=17i$.
Now take the conjugate of that product.
The right side says take the conjugates first. Write each one.
Multiply them out term by term.
Replace $i^{2}$ by $-1$ and collect. The real numbers give $6-12=-6$, and the $i$ terms give $-9i-8i=-17i$.
From $(1)$ and $(2)$ both sides agree.

written.say: Calculate the left side first: perform the operation before conjugating. Multiply each term in the first bracket by each term in the second.
Take the conjugate of this result.
For the right side, conjugate the two inputs first.
Multiply each term in the first bracket by each term in the second.
Both sides give $-6-17i$, so the required equality holds for these values.

parts.label: (iii)
parts.question: $\overline{\left(\frac{z_{1}}{z_{2}}\right)}=\frac{\bar{z_{1}}}{\bar{z_{2}}}$
parts.answer: Both sides give $\dfrac{18}{13}+\dfrac{1}{13}i$, so the property holds.

steps.why: The left side says divide first, then take the conjugate. Begin with the division.
There is an $i$ in the denominator, so multiply the top and the bottom by the conjugate of the bottom, which is $2-3i$.
Work out the numerator, multiplying term by term.
Replace $i^{2}$ by $-1$. Note $-12i^{2}=12$, so the real numbers give $6+12=18$, and the $i$ terms give $-9i+8i=-i$.
Work out the denominator, of the form $(a+b)(a-b)=a^{2}-b^{2}$.
Put the numerator over the denominator and split it into two parts.
Now take the conjugate of that, changing the sign of the imaginary part only.
Turn to the right side, which says take the conjugates first, then divide.
Multiply the top and the bottom by the conjugate of the new bottom, which is $2+3i$.
Work out the numerator, then replace $i^{2}$ by $-1$. Here $6+12=18$ and $9i-8i=i$.
The denominator is the same pair of brackets as before, so it is $13$ again.
So the right side comes to this.
From $(1)$ and $(2)$ both sides agree, and this is the common value.

written.say: Calculate the left side first: perform the operation before conjugating. Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate $2-3i$.
Expand the numerator first.
Multiply the conjugate pair using the difference of squares.
Substitute the numerator and denominator, then simplify to rectangular form.
Take the conjugate of this result.
For the right side, conjugate the two inputs first.
Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate $2+3i$.
Expand the numerator first.
Multiply the conjugate pair using the difference of squares.
Substitute the numerator and denominator, then simplify to rectangular form.
Both sides give $\dfrac{18}{13}+\dfrac{1}{13}i$, so the required equality holds for these values.

parts.label: (iv)
parts.question: $|z_{1}|=\left|-\bar{z_{1}}\right|$
parts.answer: Both sides give $5$, so the property holds.

steps.why: Start with the plain modulus. The modulus of $z=x+iy$ is $\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}$, and here $x=3$ and $y=4$.
Square each part, add them, and take the root. Since $5\times 5=25$, the root is exact.
Now build $-\bar{z_{1}}$ in two moves. First take the conjugate, which changes the sign of the imaginary part only.
Then put a minus in front of that, which changes the sign of both parts.
Take its modulus, with $x=-3$ and $y=4$.
Square each part. The minus sign disappears, because minus times minus gives plus.
From $(1)$ and $(2)$ both are the same. Changing signs never changes how far a point is from the origin.

written.say: The real and imaginary coefficients are $3$ and $4$. Use the nonnegative square root.
Keep the real coefficient and change the sign of the imaginary coefficient.
Negate the conjugate by changing both signs.
The real and imaginary coefficients are $-3$ and $4$. Use the nonnegative square root.
The two distances are equal.

steps.why: Take the conjugate of $z_{2}$ once. Keep the real part and change the sign of the imaginary part.
Now take the conjugate again, of the number just found. The real part $2$ stays, and the imaginary part $-3$ changes sign to $+3$.
That is the number we started with, so the property holds.

written.say: Keep the real coefficient and change the sign of the imaginary coefficient.
Conjugate once more; the imaginary sign changes back.

notes.watchOut: On the complex plane this says that reflecting a point in the real axis twice brings it back to where it started.

parts.label: (vi)
parts.question: $z_{1}\bar{z_{1}}=|z_{1}|^{2}$
parts.answer: Both sides give $25$, so the property holds.

steps.why: Write the conjugate of $z_{1}$ first, changing the sign of the imaginary part.
Multiply $z_{1}$ by $\bar{z_{1}}$. The two brackets are of the form $(a+b)(a-b)$, which is always $a^{2}-b^{2}$.
Open the second square, squaring both the $4$ and the $i$.
Subtract. Taking away $-16$ is the same as adding $16$, so the answer is an ordinary real number.
Now the other side. Find the modulus, using $|z|=\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}$ with $x=3$ and $y=4$.
Square that modulus, because the right side asks for $|z_{1}|^{2}$, not $|z_{1}|$.
From $(1)$ and $(2)$ both sides give the same number.

written.say: Keep the real coefficient and change the sign of the imaginary coefficient.
For the left side, multiply the conjugate pair.
For the right side, use the modulus of the original number.
Square the modulus, as the right side requires.
The two sides agree.

notes.watchOut: The right side is $|z_{1}|^{2}$, not $|z_{1}|$. There is no square root at the end.

questions.stem: If $z_{1}=5+4i$ and $z_{2}=3+2i$, then find:

steps.why: Multiply the brackets out term by term. Each term in the first multiplies each term in the second, which gives four products.
Collect. The real numbers give $15-8=7$, and the $i$ terms give $10i+12i=22i$.

written.say: Multiply each term in the first bracket by each term in the second.

steps.why: Write the division as a fraction. There is an $i$ in the denominator, so multiply the top and the bottom by the conjugate of the bottom, which is $3-2i$.
Work out the numerator, multiplying term by term.
Replace $i^{2}$ by $-1$. Note that $-8i^{2}=8$, because minus times minus gives plus.
Collect. The real numbers give $15+8=23$, and the $i$ terms give $-10i+12i=2i$.
Work out the denominator, of the form $(a+b)(a-b)=a^{2}-b^{2}$.
Put the numerator over the denominator and split it into two parts.

written.say: Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate $3-2i$.
Expand the numerator first.
Multiply the conjugate pair using the difference of squares.
Substitute the numerator and denominator, then simplify to rectangular form.

steps.why: Write both conjugates first. Keep each real part and change the sign of each imaginary part.
Multiply them out term by term.
Collect. The real numbers give $15-8=7$, and the $i$ terms give $-10i-12i=-22i$.

written.say: Write the conjugates first.
Multiply each term in the first bracket by each term in the second.

notes.shortcut: This is the conjugate of the answer to part (i), which is exactly what the property $\overline{z_{1}z_{2}}=\bar{z_{1}}\,\bar{z_{2}}$ promises.

steps.why: The product was worked out in part (i), so start from it. Its real part is $7$ and its imaginary part is $22$.
The modulus of $z=x+iy$ is $\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}$. Put the two parts into that formula.
Square each part and add, keeping everything under the one root.
Take the square root. Since $533$ is not a perfect square, the root must stay as it is.

written.say: Multiply each term in the first bracket by each term in the second.
The real and imaginary coefficients are $7$ and $22$. Use the nonnegative square root.
Since $533=13\cdot41$ has no square factor greater than $1$, the exact modulus remains $\sqrt{533}$.

notes.alsoAcceptable: $\sqrt{41}\times\sqrt{13}$ is the same number, because $|z_{1}z_{2}|=|z_{1}||z_{2}|$ and $41\times 13=533$.

questions.stem: Find the real and imaginary parts of $z=(2+7i)^{-1}$.

steps.why: A power of $-1$ means turn the number over, using $a^{-n}=\frac{1}{a^{n}}$, so write it as $1$ over the bracket.
The parts can only be read from the form $x+iy$, and there is still an $i$ in the denominator. Multiply the top and the bottom by the conjugate of the bottom, which is $2-7i$.
Work out the denominator. The two brackets are of the form $(a+b)(a-b)$, which is always $a^{2}-b^{2}$.
Square each part. Since $(7i)^{2}=49i^{2}=-49$, taking it away adds $49$.
The numerator is just $2-7i$, because the top was $1$.
Split it into a real part and an imaginary part.
Now the number is in the form $x+iy$, so read off the two parts.

written.say: Let $z=(2+7i)^{-1}$. Write the reciprocal and use the conjugate $2-7i$.
Multiply the conjugate pair using the difference of squares.
Substitute the numerator and denominator, then simplify to rectangular form.
Read the real coefficient and the coefficient of $i$.

notes.watchOut: The imaginary part is $-\frac{7}{53}$, a real number. The $i$ is never part of it.

questions.stem: Solve the given simultaneous linear equations with complex coefficients for $z$ and $w$: $\ iz+(2-i)w=4+i$ and $iz+(3+i)w=3+3i$.

steps.why: Call the two equations $(1)$ and $(2)$. Both begin with exactly the same term $iz$, so taking one from the other removes $z$ straight away. Take equation $(1)$ away from equation $(2)$.
Work out the bracket on the left. A minus in front of a bracket changes both signs, so $3-2=1$ and $i+i=2i$.
Work out the right side the same way. $3-4=-1$ and $3i-i=2i$.
So the $z$ terms have gone and one unknown is left.
Divide both sides by $1+2i$, then clear the $i$ by multiplying the top and the bottom by the conjugate $1-2i$.
Work out the numerator, multiplying term by term.
Replace $i^{2}$ by $-1$. Note $-4i^{2}=4$, so the real numbers give $-1+4=3$, and the $i$ terms give $2i+2i=4i$.
Work out the denominator, of the form $(a+b)(a-b)=a^{2}-b^{2}$.
So $w$ is this fraction. Split it into two parts.
Now go back to equation $(1)$ for $z$. Work out the term $(2-i)w$ first.
Multiply the top out term by term.
Replace $i^{2}$ by $-1$. Note $-4i^{2}=4$, so the real numbers give $6+4=10$, and the $i$ terms give $8i-3i=5i$.
Divide each term by $5$.
Take this away from both sides of equation $(1)$, so only $iz$ is left.
Work out the right side. $4-2=2$ and $i-i=0$, so the answer is a plain real number.
Divide both sides by $i$, then clear the $i$ from the bottom by multiplying the top and the bottom by $i$.
Replace $i^{2}$ by $-1$. Dividing by $-1$ just changes the sign.
State both answers.

written.say: Label the two original equations.
Both equations open with the same term $iz$, so subtracting $(1)$ from $(2)$ removes $z$ at once.
Clear both brackets. A minus in front changes every sign inside.
Divide by $1+2i$, then clear the $i$ with the conjugate $1-2i$.
Now back to equation $(1)$ for $z$, starting with the term $(2-i)w$.
Take that from both sides of equation $(1)$, leaving $iz$ on its own.
Divide by $i$, then clear the $i$ from the bottom by multiplying top and bottom by $i$.
Thus the solution is

check.why: Both original equations hold after substituting the values of $z$ and $w$.

notes.shortcut: Subtracting is quicker than substituting here, because the $z$ terms are already identical. Look for that before rearranging anything.

questions.stem: Solve $(3-4i)(a+bi)=1+0i$ and find the values of $a$ and $b$. Assume $a$ and $b$ are real.

steps.why: The left side is not yet split into a real part and an imaginary part, so multiply the brackets out term by term. Here $a$ and $b$ are real numbers.
Replace $i^{2}$ by $-1$. Note that $-4bi^{2}=4b$, because minus times minus gives plus.
Collect the terms with no $i$ into one bracket and the terms with $i$ into another, taking $i$ out as a common factor.
Two complex numbers are equal only when their real parts match and their imaginary parts match. Compare the real parts first, and number the result.
Now compare the imaginary parts. The right side is $1+0i$, so its imaginary part is $0$.
Rearrange equation $(2)$ to get $b$ on its own. Add $4a$ to both sides, then divide both sides by $3$.
Put this in place of $b$ in equation $(1)$, so only $a$ is left.
Work out the second term. Multiplying $\frac{4a}{3}$ by $4$ gives $\frac{16a}{3}$.
Multiply every term by $3$ to clear the fraction.
Add the two terms on the left.
Divide both sides by $25$.
Put this value back into $b=\frac{4a}{3}$.
The two $3$s cancel.
State both answers.

written.say: Multiply the left side out term by term. Both $a$ and $b$ are real.
Equal complex numbers match part for part, and the right side is $1+0i$.
Make $b$ the subject of $(2)$.
Put that into $(1)$, so only $a$ is left.
Put that value back into $b=\frac{4a}{3}$.
Thus the solution is

check.why: Put the two values back in. The brackets give $a^{2}-b^{2}$ with $a=3$ and $b=4i$, which comes to $25$, so the answer is $1$.

notes.shortcut: The question is really asking for the multiplicative inverse of $3-4i$, because $a+bi$ is what $3-4i$ must be multiplied by to give $1$.

questions.stem: Solve the equation for $x$ and $y$: $\ (3-2i)(x+yi)=2(x-2yi)+2i-1$. Assume $x$ and $y$ are real.

steps.why: Neither side is split into a real part and an imaginary part yet, so open the brackets on both sides. Take the left side first, multiplying term by term. Here $x$ and $y$ are real numbers.
Replace $i^{2}$ by $-1$. Note that $-2yi^{2}=2y$, because minus times minus gives plus.
Collect the terms with no $i$ and the terms with $i$, taking $i$ out as a common factor.
Now the right side. Open the bracket, multiplying each term inside by $2$.
Collect it the same way. The terms with no $i$ are $2x$ and $-1$, and the terms with $i$ are $-4yi$ and $2i$.
Two complex numbers are equal only when both parts match. Compare the real parts first.
Take $2x$ from both sides to gather the $x$ terms, and number the result.
Now compare the imaginary parts.
Add $4y$ to both sides to gather the $y$ terms, and number the result.
Rearrange equation $(1)$ to get $x$ on its own, by taking $2y$ from both sides. We choose $x$ because it has no number in front, which keeps the working simple.
Put this in place of $x$ in equation $(2)$, so only $y$ is left.
Open the bracket. Minus times minus gives plus, so $-2\times(-1)=2$ and $-2\times(-2y)=4y$.
Add the two $y$ terms.
Take $2$ from both sides.
Divide both sides by $11$. $0$ shared between any number of parts is still $0$.
Put $y=0$ back into $x=-1-2y$. Twice $0$ is $0$, so nothing is taken away.
State both answers.

written.say: Open the left side term by term. Both $x$ and $y$ are real.
Now the right side, opened and collected the same way.
Equal complex numbers match part for part. Compare the real parts.
Then compare the imaginary parts.
In $(1)$ the letter $x$ carries no number in front, so make it the subject.
Put that into $(2)$, so only $y$ is left.
Put that back into $x=-1-2y$.
Thus the solution is

check.why: Put $x=-1$ and $y=0$ into each side on its own. Both come to $-3+2i$, so the answers are correct.

notes.watchOut: The value $y=0$ is a valid solution, not an omitted answer. It says the number $x+yi$ turns out to be the real number $-1$.
